Here's something that might surprise you: when you type a message to an AI, it never actually reads your words.

Not a single letter.

What it reads instead are *numbers* — and getting there is weirder than most people expect.

---

**Tokenization** is the first thing that happens to your prompt.

The model doesn't split your text into letters or even words — it splits it into *tokens*, which are chunks that roughly correspond to common syllables, word-pieces, or whole short words.

[EX]The word "tokenization" might become three tokens: "token", "ization" — wait, actually "token" + "iz" + "ation". The word "cat" is probably one token. A rare word like "Svalbard" might get chopped into four. GPT-4 uses a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 possible tokens.[/EX]

Each token then gets converted to a number — its ID in the vocabulary list.

So your sentence becomes a list of integers before the model ever "thinks" about it.

[KEY]Your words are immediately converted into number sequences (tokens), because neural networks only do math — they can't process raw text.[/KEY]

Here's a quick check on that:

[Q]
The sentence "I went to the bank" is tricky for a tokenizer. Why?
A) The tokenizer can't handle sentences longer than four words
B) The word "bank" maps to one token, but that token could mean a riverbank or a financial institution — the model needs context to know which
C) "Bank" is too rare a word to have a token
ANS: B
[/Q]

It sees three pieces: **"un"**, **"believ"**, **"able"** — each one a number.

That's because the first thing an LLM does is break your text into **tokens** — chunks that are somewhere between a letter and a word. Every token gets converted to a number, and that number is what the model actually processes. GPT-4 has a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 of these tokens.

[KEY]Tokens are the basic unit an LLM reads — not letters, not words, but numbered chunks that can be parts of words.[/KEY]

[EX]The sentence "I went to the bank" might become 6 tokens: "I", " went", " to", " the", " bank", "." — each mapped to a unique number before the model touches it.[/EX]

Here's why this matters: the word "bank" is just one number. The model has no idea yet whether you mean a riverbank or a financial institution. That ambiguity lives in the number — and the model has to figure out meaning from context.

[Q]
What does an LLM actually receive as input after you type a prompt?
A) The exact words you typed, read left to right like a human
B) A sequence of numbers, each representing a token (chunk of text)
C) A search query sent to a database of facts
ANS: B
[/Q]
